question.prompt: In multiplying two positive integers \(a\) and \(b,\) Ron reversed the digits of the two-digit number \(a.\) His erroneous product was \(161.\) What is the correct value of the product of \(a\) and \(b?\)

solutions.explanation:
The number Ron actually multiplied must be a factor of \(161\). Let that reversed number be \(R\). Reversing a two-digit number gives a value between \(1\) and \(99\) if a leading zero is allowed. Since
\[
161=7\cdot23
\]
and both factors are prime, its positive factors are \(1,7,23,161\). Thus the only possible values of \(R\) are \(1,7,23\).

Under the convention that the reversal must remain a two-digit number, only \(R=23\) is possible. Then \(a=32\), \(b=7\), and the correct product is
\[
ab=32\cdot7=\boxed{224},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

The displayed wording does not explicitly impose that convention. If leading zeros are allowed after reversal, \(R=1\) comes from \(a=10\), with \(b=161\), giving the correct product \(1610\). Also, \(R=7\) comes from \(a=70\), with \(b=23\), again giving \(1610\). These exhaust the possible reversed factors.

Therefore the products permitted by the literal wording are \(\boxed{224\text{ and }1610}\). The keyed choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\) requires the additional two-digit-reversal convention.
solutions.title: Check every possible reversed factor
